title: MB9-11057
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They are appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting their claims for refugee protection based on credibility.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (principal appellant) and her minor daughter, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (associate appellant) are Haitian citizens. They are appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting their claims for refugee protection based on credibility.

The associate appellant's refugee protection claim is based on the allegations in the principal appellant's Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form) that she fears returning to Haiti because of her political opinion and domestic violence.
The determinative issue is whether the RPD erred in its assessment of the appellants' credibility.
I find that the appellants are not credible and that the RPD's decision is correct. The appeal is dismissed.

In her BOC Form, the principal appellant alleges that her husband is a political activist and member of the VÚritÚ [Truth] political party, and that he ran for Port-au-Prince's third electoral district in the 2014-2015 elections. She alleges that she rallied alongside her husband during the election campaign. She alleges that she was appointed first XXXX at the Haitian embassy in the Dominican Republic on May 12, 2016, under Mr. Privert's interim government. On February 7, 2017, Mr. Moise became president and the principal appellant was dismissed from her position on June 16, 2017. On September 12, 2017, she took part in an anti-government demonstration to protest against the cost of living and rising oil prices and to support a higher minimum wage. On September 14, 2017, three armed individuals allegedly broke into her home, abused her, struck her and threatened to kidnap and rape her. Her husband then allegedly drove her to the hospital and, after she was treated, he drove her to her sister's place. The following day, her brother-in-law allegedly brought her to the police station to file a complaint. On XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, she left the country for the Dominican Republic, and then arrived in Canada in XXXX 2017. The day of the hearing, she added new allegations of domestic violence.

The Minister intervened in the appellants' claims for refugee protection, requesting that they be rejected on grounds of credibility. I note that the Minister did not intervene in the appeal. EVIDENCE PRODUCED AFTER THE APPEAL WAS PERFECTED

After her appeal was perfected, the principal appellant filed documents, that is, a divorce certificate along with an excerpt of the divorce judgment. The principal appellant sent these documents to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD), stating only the following: [translation] "Please accept an important exhibit for the record of the above-mentioned appellant. It is the certificate issued from her divorce from her spouse, as she requested."

First, I want to point out that the RAD sent a letter to the principal appellant and to her legal counsel requesting that they submit an application under rules 29 and 37 of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules (RAD Rules). The RAD did not receive any response in this respect. A reminder letter was sent to the principal appellant and her legal counsel to remedy this failure, including a request to provide the full copy of the divorce judgment, but the RAD did not receive anything.

According to subrule 29(2) of the RAD Rules, if the principal appellant wants to use a document that was not previously provided, she must make an application to the RAD in accordance with rule 37. Moreover, under the provisions of subrule 29(3), the application includes an explanation of how the document meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and how that evidence relates to the principal appellant. Furthermore, according to subrule 37(4), any evidence that the principal appellant wants the RAD to consider must be given in an affidavit. I am of the opinion that the evidence provided does not comply with the rules mentioned, and in the absence of an affidavit or a statutory declaration and of a full copy of the divorce judgment, I am unable to examine the principal appellant's allegations regarding the divorce granted, including the allegations in the divorce judgment. The documents filed do not alleviate the concerns raised. I want to point out that the divorce certificate indicates that the divorce judgment was granted on April 19, 2019, and the principal appellant did not explain why this document was not filed prior to the rejection of the refugee protection claim on May 6, 2019.

Beyond this formality, and in deciding whether to allow an application provided under rule 29, the RAD must consider any relevant factors, including the document's relevance and probative value, any new evidence the document brings to the appeal, and whether the appellant, with reasonable effort, could have provided the document with the record.1 With respect to subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, it was held in Singh that the express provisions of that subsection are inescapable, have to be met and leave no room for discretion on the part of the RAD. It also held that the implicit admissibility criteria set out in Raza2 also result from the wording of subsection 110(4).3
I note that it appears that the evidence produced can be considered relevant in assessing the prospective risk and the principal appellant's profile as a single woman.

However, with respect to the probative value of this evidence, I note that the excerpt from the divorce judgment, which was appended to the divorce certificate, shows that the court granted the principal appellant's divorce [translation] "for serious and public abuse" against her husband. However, the principal appellant stated at the hearing that she learned in December 2018 that her husband was having an extramarital affair with a girl in the Dominican Republic. Consequently, she stated that she wanted to initiate a divorce for [translation] "infidelity." The principal appellant's statements therefore contradict the content of the excerpt from the divorce judgment. I also note that the excerpt of the divorce judgment and the divorce certificate have the same signature, namely, that of the civil registrar, despite the fact that the divorce judgment was made by a Haitian court judge. In light of these inconsistencies, I am of the opinion that these documents have no probative value.

I note that the principal appellant did not explain whether she had made reasonable efforts to obtain or submit a copy of the divorce judgment in support of her memorandum of appeal, despite the letters that were sent to her in this regard.
For all of these reasons, I consider that the documents produced are not admissible as new evidence.

The appellants submitted a request for an oral hearing in support of their appeal. Given that the new evidence is inadmissible, the RAD shall proceed without holding an oral hearing. The request for an oral hearing is rejected.

In accordance with Huruglica4 and Rozas del Solar,5 I conducted my own assessment of all of the evidence, including the audio recording of the hearing, and I applied the correctness standard. ANALYSIS Event of September 14, 2017
paragraphs.heading_before: ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

paragraphs.text: In her BOC Form, the principal appellant alleges that on September 14, 2017, her husband came home with three of his friends. Having a swollen eye, redness on her arms and pain, she was driven to the hospital by her husband and then brought to her mother's house. Her daughter was driven to her sister's house by her husband's brother. However, at the hearing, the principal appellant stated that she put ice over her eye and went to the hospital the day after the incident. She stated that she had stayed with her neighbour between September 14 and 19, 2017, and then went to her sister's house. When asked about these contradictions, the principal appellant maintained her testimony.

The RPD did not accept the principal appellant's explanation and was of the opinion that the discrepancies between the BOC Form and her testimony call into question the events following the incident of September 14, 2017. It believed that these contradictions were significant and undermined the occurrence of this incident, as well as the subsequent steps at the hospital. The RPD found that the principal appellant's testimony was not credible or trustworthy.

In her memorandum of appeal, the principal appellant submits that her testimony was true as was ruled in Maldonado.6 She submits that despite flaws regarding the incident of September 14, 2017, likely on account of her emotional state, this attack could have conceivably occurred. She submits that immigration decision-makers must demonstrate a certain sensitivity and tact when intervening with refugee protection claimants, who are people that come from diverse cultures and backgrounds, who have experienced somewhat tragic situations and who are appearing before a panel for the first time to testify.

First, I must specify that the principal appellant did not file any medical or psychological evidence on her psychological state and her ability to testify at the hearing. Therefore, it seems to me that the principal appellant's nervousness and emotional situation do not satisfactorily justify the significant contradictions raised by the RPD. Consequently, I do not accept her claim that her emotional state affected her testimony. I would add that the principal appellant did not raise any arguments before the RPD about difficulties testifying because of her emotional state, so that it could make the appropriate procedural accommodations.

I note that the principal appellant's testimony at the hearing contradicts the events noted in her written account. First, she stated at the hearing that she had put ice over her eye and went to the hospital the day after the incident of September 14, 2017,7 contrary to what is indicated in her written account, which states that her husband brought her to the hospital the day of the incident. Her testimony at the hearing, that she stayed with her neighbour between September 14 and 19, 2017, also contradicts her written account, which states that she went to her sister's house after receiving hospital care. There is no mention in the written account of her stay with the neighbour. I agree with the RPD and consider the contradictions raised to be significant. I want to point out that the incident of September 14, 2017, is the crucial element that forced the principal appellant to flee her country. The RPD's negative finding on the principal appellant's credibility regarding the occurrence of this event is correct. Complaint to the police

In her BOC Form, the principal appellant indicated that the day after the incident mentioned above, her brother-in-law brought her to the police station to file a complaint. At the hearing, however, she stated that it was her brother-in-law who filed the complaint without her since she had stayed in bed at her sister's house for a week. At the hearing, she submitted a copy of a police certificate8 that shows that she made the complaint, with no mention of the brother-in-law's presence. When asked about these contradictions, the principal appellant stated that she was not in a normal state when she made the complaint with the police. She added that she did not remember whether her brother-in-law had gone to the police station with her.9

The RPD was of the opinion that the principal appellant's explanation did not clarify the contradictions between the BOC Form, her testimony and the evidence submitted. It considered that the principal appellant provided three different versions of the complaint filed at the police station. It found that these versions cannot be reconciled and that the principal appellant's overall credibility was seriously undermined.

I note that this finding and the RPD's other negative findings on the principal appellant's credibility are uncontested in the memorandum of appeal, and I do not see the RPD's alleged error in this matter. Allegations of domestic violence

The RPD asked the principal appellant why she did not mention this fear in her initial account or amend her BOC Form to include her allegation of domestic violence, and she stated that the decision to leave her husband was a difficult one, and that he was on the telephone when she completed her BOC Form. She stated that the decision to separate from her husband was made in December 2018, nearly three months before the date of the hearing.

The RPD was of the opinion that the principal appellant did not provide a reasonable explanation for the delay in reporting that she would fear her husband if she returned to Haiti. The RPD noted that the principal appellant had been represented by her legal counsel since her BOC Form was signed in December 2017, and that she was represented by the same counsel at the hearing. Given its finding on the principal appellant's overall credibility, the RPD concluded that she failed to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, the truthfulness of her allegations that she was a victim of domestic violence.

In her memorandum of appeal, the principal appellant submits that she gave a compelling and convincing testimony of the violence she suffered from her husband. She submits that there is no reason to doubt the information she provided at the last minute out of fear of reprisal if ever she had to return to Haiti and if her husband were to find out about it. She states that she was aware that her husband spoke quite frequently with her legal counsel (in this case in Canada) and that he had selected and paid him. She claims that, in her submissions, her legal counsel discusses the rather troubling and even dangerous situation that she was in. She states that she had informed her legal counsel of her decision to separate, but it was only on the day of the hearing that she resigned herself to telling him about the domestic violence she suffered. She submits that the RPD's conclusions are unfair with regard to her social and marital situation. The RPD was influenced by the negative inferences drawn from the events of September 14, 2017. The RPD demonstrated an extreme lack of sensitivity.
I want to point out that in its decision, the RPD stated that it had considered the allegations of domestic violence put forward by the principal appellant at her hearing.

I note that in paragraph 5 of her memorandum of appeal, in the arguments section,10 the principal appellant states that she had sent a note to the RPD, notifying it [translation] "of her decision to separate from her husband as of that date." However, after examining all of the evidence, I note that there is no evidence in this regard on the record, as claimed by the principal appellant.

Considering that the principal appellant raised allegations of domestic violence, I must specify that I considered Chairperson's Guideline 4,11 including the fact that women may be reluctant to provide details on the persecution they experienced. In this case, the principal appellant stated that, on the day of the hearing, she told her legal counsel about the episodes of domestic violence she suffered from her spouse, and yet there were no amendments made that same day to include these allegations that were omitted from the account and that are, in fact, important. If the principal appellant was reluctant to speak to her legal counsel about the domestic violence, she did not explain why she decided to tell him about it the day of the hearing, and also why she did not amend her account before declaring at the start of the hearing that the content of her BOC Form was complete, true, correct and up-to-date. In Lawani,12 the Federal Court ruled as follows: 33. I also do not agree with Ms. Lawani's contention that the RPD erred in drawing negative inferences from the late presentation of her bisexuality claim. The RPD has flexibility in examining factors affecting credibility. It did not believe Ms. Lawani's explanation for the last-minute addition of her bisexuality claim, and explained why in great details in its decision, taking into account the fact that Ms. Lawani was in Canada for a long period before her refugee claim was examined by the RPD.

I do not agree with the principal appellant's contention that the RPD was influenced by the other negative inferences about credibility. The RPD provided a detailed analysis explaining why it did not accept the principal appellant's explanations regarding the allegations of domestic violence. The RPD's analysis in this respect is separate from that which allowed it to reject the principal appellant's allegations in her written account for lack of credibility. With that, I am of the opinion that the RPD did not err in concluding that the principal appellant did not establish the truthfulness of her allegations regarding domestic violence. Its conclusion is correct. Gender-based risk

The RPD considered that the principal appellant did not face similar circumstances as those of women who are single and at risk in Haiti. It was of the opinion that the principal appellant is a married woman and therefore cannot be considered a single woman without male protection. It added that even if it accepted the principal appellant's allegation that she is separated from her husband, her mother and sister live in Carrefour and her family would welcome her with open arms if she returned to Haiti. It considered that the principal appellant is an educated woman who could work, and that she would have access to housing and family support in Haiti. It concluded that the principal appellant did not establish a reasonable fear of gender-related persecution.

In her memorandum of appeal, the principal appellant submits that the RPD should have considered that, if she returned to Haiti, she would be persecuted because of her alleged political opinion and her husband's political activities. She states that the RPD should have also considered her fear because of her status as a single young woman without resources. The RPD should have also considered her fear of being defenceless in a situation of domestic violence. She submits that domestic violence and violence against women are endemic and tolerated in Haiti. She states that the RPD's conclusion that she is considered a married woman who has male protection is exaggerated and seemingly arbitrary. She adds that her parents are disabled, that her family lives in a dangerous neighbourhood, namely, Martissant, and that she provided for her family's needs with help from her husband. The RPD therefore erred in assessing her socio-economic situation. She submits that her husband would have trouble accepting her decision to separate and that she would one day have to return to live with him and continue to suffer from domestic violence because of her financial dependence on him. As for the possibility of finding employment, the RPD did not consider Haiti's high unemployment rate or her allegation that she got the embassy position because of her husband's political influence. She submits that despite the flaws undermining her credibility, the fact remains that her situation subjects her to a high risk of gender-related persecution and domestic violence.
I note that the RPD considered the objective evidence on the situation of women at risk of physical and sexual violence in Haiti13 and the principal appellant's particular situation.

I note that the principal appellant alleges that she was targeted because of her political opinion and also because she is a single woman in Haiti. I want to point out that the principal appellant is educated, has worked in Haiti and at one time held the first secretary position at the Haitian embassy in the Dominican Republic. The principal appellant's two brothers and her father still live in Haiti. I want to point out that the principal appellant did not allege before the RPD that her parents have a disability and did not produce new evidence in this respect. I am therefore of the opinion that the principal appellant has male protection and that her profile does not correspond to that of women at risk, especially those who are uneducated and do not have male protection. I would add that the RPD provided a detailed analysis based on the evidence regarding gender-based sexual violence, and rightly concluded that it is a problem in Haiti. The RPD compared the principal appellant's profile with that of groups of at-risk women in Haiti, namely, young women, elderly women and those living in precarious homes, and I am of the opinion that it correctly concluded that she is not a member of any of these groups.

In Dezameau,14 the Federal Court mentioned that membership in a particular social group is not sufficient to result in a finding of persecution. The evidence provided must still satisfy the decision-maker that there is a risk of harm that is sufficiently serious and whose occurrence is "more than a mere possibility."

Given that the principal appellant failed to establish her membership in one of these groups of at-risk women who are more likely to be victims of gender-based violence, I am of the opinion that she failed to establish that the risk of gender-based violence in Haiti would be more than a mere possibility, and I conclude that the RPD's conclusion in this respect is correct.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the determination, according to which the appellants are neither "Convention refugees" nor "persons in need of protection."
